profile.title: Nutrition Counseling for Hypertension and Severe Obesity in a Precontemplative Patient with Minimized Alcohol Intake
profile.summary: This case trains dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment and MI-based counseling session with a precontemplative, blunt patient who has essential hypertension and severe obesity but minimizes both her alcohol intake and her antihypertensive nonadherence. The core teaching points are eliciting an accurate alcohol/diet history through specific non-judgmental questioning, spotting a patient-versus-chart mismatch (self-reported 'a glass here and there' versus documentation suggesting a much heavier weekend pattern), and building a PES statement and realistic, patient-centered plan rather than lecturing a patient who feels dismissed by both her family and the healthcare system.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Bridgewater, New Jersey (on a short break between helping with household chores, in a cluttered shared living room)

patient.name: Annamae Hauck
patient.occupation: Billing coordinator at a regional orthopedic practice
patient.appearance: Severely obese body habitus, facial fullness, sitting slightly tilted to favor her lower back, dressed in work-casual clothes with a lanyard still around her neck as if she just stepped away from her desk; background shows a busy, cluttered living room with sounds of family members occasionally passing through.

persona.personality: Blunt, impatient, no-nonsense; sharp and matter-of-fact, mildly defensive about her weight and drinking, takes pride in knowing her own numbers
persona.communicationStyle: Precise and factual, cites her own lab values and dates readily, gets irritated by vague or 'preachy' explanations, softens slightly when she feels heard rather than judged
persona.emotionalState: Mildly defensive and impatient, with underlying fatigue and resignation about her health being 'just how it is', becomes more open if approached without judgment
persona.background: Annamae grew up in a loud, bustling central New Jersey family where meals were whatever could be thrown together between someone's shift and someone's practice. She's worked as a billing coordinator at a regional orthopedic practice for years, is proud of how organized she keeps her medical appointments and medication schedule, and currently lives in a crowded house with seven family members she describes as 'loud and unhelpful' about her health. She keeps a small succulent on her desk ('the only thing I haven't managed to kill'), unwinds most evenings with true crime documentaries, and has a standing Friday takeout order from the same Italian deli she's used for years.
speechExamples: My pressure was 97 over 64 last time, so I don't really get why we're doing this again.
Look, I don't cook for one person, it's a waste of time and money.
It's genetic, half my family is built this way, no amount of salad is changing that.
I have a glass of wine here and there, nothing crazy.
I don't need a lecture, I need you to tell me something I don't already know.
concerns: Being told to overhaul her whole diet when she feels she doesn't have time to cook
Her weight being blamed for everything from her back pain to her blood pressure
Being lectured by someone younger than her kids

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition counseling visit with Annamae Hauck, a 46-year-old woman referred for nutrition counseling related to blood pressure and weight management. Review her available health record before the visit. Your job is to complete a nutrition assessment, understand her eating and drinking patterns and barriers, and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Nutrition counseling visit for blood pressure and weight management
scenario.openingLine: Hi, I'm here for the nutrition thing, but honestly my pressure was 97 over 64 last time so I'm not sure what we're fixing. Let's just get through this.
tasks: Take a focused diet, fluid, and alcohol history using specific, non-judgmental questioning techniques
Review available vitals, labs, and chart/pharmacy documentation and compare them with what the patient reports
Assess the patient's readiness to change and identify her personal goals and barriers around eating, drinking, and medication-taking
Develop at least one nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) addressing her presenting concerns
Deliver brief, patient-centered nutrition education or counseling using a motivational interviewing approach, and propose one realistic next step

objectives.text: Elicit a specific, non-judgmental alcohol history and compare the patient's self-report with prior documentation to identify discrepancies in reported versus actual intake
Assess the patient's stage of readiness to change and apply motivational interviewing techniques appropriate to a precontemplative patient, linking counseling to her own stated goals
Evaluate sodium, portion size, and meal timing patterns in a convenience-food-based diet and connect findings to the patient's hypertension and lipid profile
Identify medication adherence gaps (hydrochlorothiazide) and related patient-reported barriers, and compare them against pharmacy refill history
Explore how a dismissive, chaotic household environment and sedentary occupation act as barriers to dietary and activity change
Formulate at least one nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) integrating diet history, alcohol intake, vitals, and lab data, and propose a realistic, patient-centered next step

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive sodium/energy intake from convenience foods and underreported alcohol use in the context of essential hypertension and severe obesity, in a precontemplative patient
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive sodium intake related to high reliance on convenience/frozen/deli foods as evidenced by frequent frozen dinners, deli sandwiches, and takeout subs and diagnosis of essential hypertension

Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive alcohol intake related to underreported weekend wine consumption as evidenced by patient admission of escalating pattern on questioning and discrepancy with prior documentation
Nutrition diagnosis: Overweight/obesity (excessive energy intake) related to large late-night meals and skipped breakfast as evidenced by BMI 45.3 kg/m2 and reported meal pattern

Medication adherence barrier (not a nutrition diagnosis but relevant context): hydrochlorothiazide underuse related to activity-schedule conflict as evidenced by patient-reported skipping and refill history
keyFindings: BMI 45.3 kg/m2 (height 153.2 cm, weight 106.3 kg) consistent with severe obesity
BP 97/64 mmHg on 2026-01-12, which the patient cites as reassuring but does not reflect her hypertension history or medication adherence gaps
Total cholesterol 293.3 mg/dL and LDL 216.2 mg/dL (2026-01-12), both elevated and unaddressed by patient

Diet pattern: skipped/rushed breakfast, desk-eaten deli lunch, large late convenience dinner (frozen lasagna, rotisserie chicken, takeout subs), pretzels/chips, minimal vegetables, several diet sodas daily, 'doesn't really do water'
Initial report of 'a glass here and there' of wine progressing on specific questioning to 'about two glasses most weeknights, a third on weekends'

Hidden pattern (only inferable via chart/record review, not stated by patient): documentation suggesting weekend wine intake closer to a full bottle over the past year, inconsistent with her verbal report
Hydrochlorothiazide adherence gap framed by patient as occasional forgetfulness ('once a week'), with refill record showing two late refills this year not fully disclosed by her
Precontemplative stage: patient does not connect her weight or diet to her hypertension, back pain, or UTIs; attributes weight to genetics
Family environment is dismissive/teasing about her eating and weight, reducing her motivation to change
plan: Complete a focused ADIME-format nutrition assessment: diet history (24-hour recall/typical day), meal pattern, fluid intake, alcohol use with specific non-judgmental questions, and medication-taking patterns as they relate to nutrition/lifestyle
Review available vitals, labs, and chart/pharmacy documentation for consistency with patient self-report, specifically alcohol-related documentation and hydrochlorothiazide refill history
Formulate at least one PES statement addressing excess sodium/convenience food intake and one addressing alcohol intake relative to hypertension and obesity

Use motivational interviewing (open-ended questions, reflective listening, avoid lecturing) to assess readiness to change and identify one small, patient-chosen behavior change tied to her stated goal of staying functional at work
Provide brief, non-judgmental education on sodium content of her usual convenience foods and the relationship between alcohol, blood pressure, and weight, without insisting she quit wine entirely
Plan a follow-up nutrition visit to monitor blood pressure trend, weight, and any behavior change attempted, and coordinate with her PCP regarding medication adherence barriers she disclosed
redFlags: Discrepancy between patient's self-reported alcohol intake and documentation suggestive of a heavier, undisclosed weekend drinking pattern lasting about a year
Pattern of delayed hydrochlorothiazide refills (twice this year) suggesting under-treated hypertension despite a reassuring single BP reading
Elevated LDL/total cholesterol in a patient with severe obesity and hypertension, unaddressed by patient and not yet connected to her diet
educationPoints: Explain that a single blood pressure reading does not rule out hypertension or reflect average control, especially with inconsistent medication use
Discuss sodium content of common frozen/deli/takeout foods she eats regularly and simple lower-sodium swaps that fit her time constraints
Describe how regular alcohol intake, especially larger weekend amounts, can raise blood pressure and contribute to weight gain, in neutral non-judgmental terms
Offer practical, low-effort strategies for breakfast and hydration (e.g., quick protein-containing breakfast, swapping some diet soda for water) that respect her stated dislike of cooking
Reinforce the connection between her own stated goals (staying functional at work, avoiding more medications) and small sustainable dietary changes, rather than framing changes as a moral failing

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports drinking wine 'just a glass here and there,' and when pressed, settles on about two glasses most weeknights plus a third glass on weekend nights during family gatherings (s15, s16)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Social history addendum from 11 months ago documents she drinks a bottle of wine most Saturday and Sunday nights, a pattern present for about a year (d5, a8)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may underreport alcohol intake even on repeated, non-judgmental questioning; triangulating self-report with prior documentation is essential before finalizing a nutrition diagnosis involving alcohol.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient frames her hydrochlorothiazide nonadherence as forgetting her pillbox at her sister's house about once a week, a minor and incidental lapse (s19)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows two refills in 2026 filled 9-11 days after the prior supply should have run out, indicating sustained gaps rather than occasional single missed doses (d4, a5)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient-reported adherence can understate the real pattern; refill history review helps the clinician identify a behavioral barrier (avoiding diuresis at work) that self-report alone would miss, informing counseling and referral.
